For example, when a display contains several non-target images, a researcher interested specifically in looks to the target versus a specific competitor image would code looks to the target and competitor as 1 and 0 respectively, while excluding looks to the remaining images. The onset detection method itself is compatible with any binomial coding that is appropriate for the research question.

After binarisation, we aggregate the trial-level 0/1 looks by summing across trials to obtain the number of trials coded as 1 (target_looks) and the number of trials contributing valid data (total_looks) for each participant × condition × bin combination. These binomial counts (target_looks out of total_looks) constitute the GAMM's response variablefoot_0 , and are used to model how the probability of target looks changes over time. Equivalently, one can say that the GAMM models the proportion of looks to the target image (target_looks / total_looks). However, these proportions are not precomputed for model fitting. Rather, the model is fitted directly to the binomial counts, these counts are modelled on a latent log-odds scale, and the fixation curves are obtained as predicted probabilities from the GAMM. We adopted these binarisation and aggregation processing steps for two main reasons. First, they greatly reduce the size of the dataset, reducing the computational time required for model fitting and for the simulations conducted in subsequent steps. Second, aggregating trial-level data helps reduce autocorrelation by collapsing within-trial runs of identical 0/1 observations into participant-level binomial counts, yielding a smoother and more stable timecourse of target looks.

Finally, to account for the remaining autocorrelation, we fit an autoregressive GAMM with an AR(1) term. However, because the mgcv package requires the magnitude of autocorrelation to be supplied rather than estimated, we follow a two-step approach (Van Rij et al., 2019): we first fit a GAMM with no explicit autocorrelation structure, estimate the lag-1 residual autocorrelation from that model, and then refit the same GAMM with an AR(1) term that is fixed to the estimated value.

The GAMMs employed here all included by-participant random intercepts, allowing each participant to have their own overall probability of target-looking within the analysis window, and by-participant random slopes for time, allowing participant-specific deviations in the timecourse of target looks. Additionally, each random effect was allowed to vary by condition, so that individual differences with respect to the experimental conditions could also be captured. Our models did not include random effects for items because the response variable was aggregated across items (we return to this limitation and its implications in the General Discussion).

A binomial GAMM provides two types of results that are of interest in visual world analyses. First, the parametric component provides estimates of overall target-looking (relative to non-target looks) in each experimental condition. These estimates can be considered an interpretable index of the fixation curve, in the sense introduced above. They can be used, for example, to diagnose predictive effects before the spoken presentation of a target word (e.g., Lago et al., 2023; Stone, Veríssimo, et al., 2021). Second, the GAMM includes non-linear smooth terms that model how target-looking changes over time (Miwa & Baayen, 2021; Porretta et al., 2018) (see Fig. 1, panel 1), allowing researchers to test whether trajectories differ over time across conditions (e.g., Sóskuthy, 2017; Wieling, 2018). These smooths can also be used to compute a difference curve and thereby identify time windows in which conditions differ. However, GAMM output alone does not yield a principled temporal uncertainty interval for an onset estimate, which motivates the simulation-based procedure introduced below.

Step 2: Simulating fixation curves from the fitted model

To quantify uncertainty in onset estimates, we need to account for the uncertainty in the model's predictions. In a fitted GAMM, parameters can be treated as full distributions of plausible values, rather than as fixed point estimates (D. L. Miller, 2025; Wood, 2017). We can draw values from these parameter distributions-a procedure called 'posterior simulation'-and compute, for each draw, the corresponding group-level fixation curve. This results in the simulation of many plausible fixation curves, which, taken together, capture the range of predictions implied by the fitted model (see Fig. 1, panel 2). Each simulated curve therefore represents a plausible timecourse implied by the fitted model, given the uncertainty in the estimated parameters. This simulation process is conceptually similar to the bootstrap method of Stone, Lago, and Schad (2021) in that it yields a distribution of onset estimates, but variability is generated from the fitted statistical model rather than by resampling the observed data. To obtain stable results, the analyses in Studies 1 and 2 below were based on 10,000 simulated curves. Each simulated curve is then passed to Step 3 to obtain an onset estimate.

Step 3: Establishing temporal onsets for each simulated curve

For each simulated curve, a simple onset is defined as the earliest time point at which predicted target-looking is reliably greater than its baseline value. Specifically, for each simulated fixation curve, we record the predicted value at the baseline time 𝑡 0 (on the modelled log-odds scale) and then traverse the curve from left to right. At each time point 𝑡 𝑛 , we treat the baseline value 𝜂(𝑡 0 ) as a fixed reference for that simulated curve and compute a one-sided 95% confidence interval for the predicted value at 𝑡 𝑛 from the fitted GAMM. If the lower bound of this interval at 𝑡 𝑛 exceeds 𝜂(𝑡 0 ), we record 𝑡 𝑛 as the onset (see Fig. 1, panel 3). The result of this process is a full distribution of onset times, one for each simulated curve. Note that because an onset is defined relative to the baseline time, the criterion automatically corrects for baseline differences between conditions (Barr, 2008; Barr et al., 2011).

Difference curve onsets can be obtained in the same way, but now on the basis of a contrast between two predicted fixation curves. Specifically, for each simulation draw, we compute the predicted difference curve over time. A difference curve onset is then defined as the earliest time point 𝑡 𝑛 at which the lower bound of a one-sided 95% interval for the difference curve exceeds its value at the baseline time 𝑡 0 . Conceptually, this amounts to evaluating when the two trajectories begin to diverge after aligning them at baseline. As with simple onsets, repeating this process across simulation draws yields a distribution of difference curve onsets.

We emphasise that, in our method, the criterion for onset detection is reached only when the predicted trajectory reliably exceeds the baseline value, operationalised here by the use of a one-sided confidence interval. This kind of definition has three related advantages. First, it anchors our onset criterion to evidential strength, because onsets are detected only when the baseline value is exceeded with enough certainty. This helps prevent small fluctuations due to measurement noise from being treated as onsets. Second, as is the case for sequential testing approaches (e.g., Ben-David et al., 2011; Ito et al., 2018) and for the bootstrap-based method (Stone, Lago, & Schad, 2021), our method does not require specifying an arbitrary magnitude threshold, thereby reducing researcher degrees of freedom associated with threshold selection. Third, because the criterion is standardised (i.e., tied to the standard error on the modelled scale), it is broadly portable across tasks and designs, effects of different magnitudes, and model specifications. By contrast, absolute magnitude thresholds and percent-of-maximum thresholds have often required study-specific criteria in different visual world studies (Galle et al., 2019; McMurray, Aslin, et al., 2008; Reinisch & Sjerps, 2013).

On the other hand, a limitation of using an evidence-based criterion is that onset estimates can depend on the uncertainty around the estimated fixation curves. For example, studies with greater uncertainty (e.g., with smaller sample sizes or greater variability) may yield later onsets, because greater uncertainty may delay when the criterion is satisfied. For this reason, we have additionally implemented a version of the GAMM-based method that uses a magnitude threshold, in which an onset is detected when the baseline is exceeded by a fixed amount. As a robustness check, we have additionally analysed Studies 1 and 2 with different magnitude thresholds (Appendix S1 in the Supplementary Materials). In addition, in Study 3 we evaluate how onset estimates obtained with our default criterion depend on sample size, variability, and the shape of the underlying fixation curves.

Step 4: Summarising and comparing distributions of onsets

The final step of the GAMM-based method is to summarise the onset distribution. A point estimate can be obtained using a measure of central tendency (e.g., a mean or median), whereas the uncertainty around the estimate can be quantified using an interval derived from the onset distribution (see Fig. 1, panel 4). Because onset distributions can be skewed or otherwise asymmetric, we recommend reporting medians and highest-density intervals (HDIs). A 95% HDI is the smallest contiguous region containing 95% of the distribution's mass and is less sensitive to outliers than standard quantile-based intervals (Hyndman, 1996; Kruschke & Liddell, 2018).

Once we obtain full distributions of onset estimates (for either simple onsets or difference curve onsets), onset times can be directly compared between conditions or groups. Specifically, for any contrast of interest, we take the onset estimate from each simulation draw in one condition or group and subtract the corresponding onset estimate from the same draw in the other condition or group. This process yields a paired distribution of onset differences. Summarising this distribution by its median and 95% HDI quantifies the comparison and its uncertainty. If the 95% HDI excludes zero, this provides evidence that the two onsets differ in timing.

Having outlined the four steps, we now turn to empirical applications. In Study 1, we apply the method to an existing visual world experiment to illustrate the estimation and comparison of simple onsets between two experimental conditions.

Data availability

All materials, data, and analysis code are publicly available at https://doi.org/10.17605/osf.io/9ethq.

Study 1: Estimating and comparing onsets in different conditions

This study applies the GAMM-based method to a visual world eye-tracking experiment reported by Stone, Veríssimo, et al. (2021). The authors tested the processing of German possessive pronouns, which encode both prospective (forward-looking) and retrospective (backward-looking) gender agreement dependencies. The suffix of the possessive pronoun encodes a prospective dependency, because it agrees in gender with a subsequent noun (the possessee). Meanwhile, the stem of the pronoun encodes a retrospective dependency, because it agrees in gender with a preceding antecedent noun (the possessor). For example, in Sarah fem verliert ihr fem -en masc Knopf masc 'Sarah loses her button', the pronoun ihren 'her' agrees in gender with both Knopf 'button' (the possessee) and Sarah (the antecedent or possessor).

In two visual world eye-tracking experiments, German-speaking participants heard spoken instructions such as 'Click on her blue button!', while looking at a display showing a target object (e.g., a blue button masc ) and a competitor object, with the same colour as the target object but a different grammatical gender (e.g., a blue bottle fem ). The pronoun's stem agreed in gender with the antecedent, but either matched (sein masc -en masc Knopf masc 'his button') or mismatched (ihr fem -en masc Knopf masc 'her button') the suffix's gender. Crucially, the gender of the suffix could be used to predict the identity of the target noun in both conditions. The conditions only differed in the information expressed by the pronoun stem, which was not syntactically informative for predicting the target. The key research question was whether the pronoun stem, despite being irrelevant for prediction, would nonetheless interfere with the prediction process, thus causing a processing delay in the mismatch versus match condition.

Here we focus on Stone, Veríssimo, et al.'s (2021) Experiment 2 (a higher-powered replication of their Experiment 1), which tested 74 German speakers on 96 target-competitor image pairs (each participant saw 48 trials in each condition). Stone, Veríssimo, et al. reported two analyses: a "window analysis" of proportions of looks over the whole predictive time window (from the beginning of the pronoun until the beginning of the target noun in the spoken instruction), and an onset analysis using the bootstrap-based method. The window analysis revealed that participants looked predictively at the target object in both experimental conditions, but that the predictive effect was larger in the match than in the mismatch condition. The onset analysis showed that the predictive effect started significantly earlier in the match than in the mismatch condition (mean onsets of 402 ms vs. 709 ms). Thus, the results indicated that the timecourse of predictions was influenced by the (syntactically irrelevant) antecedent agreement dependency.

We have reanalysed Stone, Veríssimo, et al.'s (2021) dataset with the GAMM-based method proposed here. We present three complementary types of results, all of which can be obtained from the same fitted model: (a) a comparison of overall proportions of target looks in the two conditions, which is akin to the window analysis reported by Stone, Veríssimo, et al.; (b) a timecourse analysis of how the fixation curves in the two conditions differ over time; and (c) an onset analysis that produces estimates of the onsets of predictive effects and their comparison between conditions.

Methods

The data were analysed with binomial (logistic) GAMMs, fitted with the mgcv R package (version 1.9-4, Wood, 2017). The dependent variable consisted of binomial counts of target (vs. competitor) looks, aggregated for each participant × condition × 20 ms bin (see above). As in Stone, Veríssimo, et al. (2021), all analyses were conducted on a predictive window that extended from the beginning of the possessive pronoun to the beginning of the target noun plus 200 ms (to account for the time taken to programme a saccade, Hallett, 1986; Salverda et al., 2014).

The GAMMs included a fixed effect of condition (sum-coded; match = -0.5; mismatch = 0.5), and a non-linear time smooth for each level of condition. Each smooth used the default basis dimension in mgcv (k = 10). Note that the choice of contrasts affects only the parametric part of the GAMM, which summarises overall target-looking across the analysis window (on the modelled log-odds scale). By contrast, the non-linear smooths are insensitive to the contrast coding of the condition fixed effect; instead, the timecourse of looks is captured by condition-specific smooths (one per condition level).

To obtain a direct inferential test of match versus mismatch timecourse differences, we additionally fitted a re-parameterised GAMM with condition coded as an ordered factor. With this parameterisation, the match condition serves as the reference smooth and the additional smooth represents the difference in timecourse between the mismatch and match conditions, yielding a p-value for this difference smooth (Wood, 2017; see also Sóskuthy, 2017; Wieling, 2018).

Models included random intercepts for participants and random slopes for condition, time, and their interaction, which were justified by model comparisons (i.e., significantly lower fREML scores: condition slopes, χ 2 (1) = 1026.10; p < .001; additional time slopes, χ 2 (1) = 5402.45; p < .001; additional condition-varying time slopes χ 2 (1) = 1045.97; p < .001). We first fitted a non-autoregressive GAMM, which displayed a lag-1 residual autocorrelation of r = 0.89; we then refitted the model with an AR(1) error structure using this value.

Results

Overall proportions.

The parametric part of the model, analogous to intercepts and slopes in a linear regression model, showed a significant intercept term (b = 0.95; z = 28.83; p < .001). Because condition was sum-coded, the parametric intercept corresponds to the mean log-odds of target (vs. competitor) looks across the match and mismatch conditions. This result indicates that comprehenders looked more to the target than to the competitor during the analysis window, suggesting that the target was predicted prior to being heard in the spoken instruction.

The condition slope-which reflects the difference between conditions in the target-over-competitor advantage-was negative, reflecting a smaller target advantage in the mismatch condition, but this difference was not statistically significant (b = -0.09; z = -1.30; p = .195).

Timecourse of looking preferences.

Table 1 shows the summary of the GAMM's smooth terms, which estimate the non-linear effects of time for each condition. The first two rows correspond to the time smooths for the match and mismatch conditions. The remaining rows correspond to by-participant random effects (intercepts and slopes). Each smooth term can be interpreted on the basis of its effective degrees of freedom (values close to 1 indicate linearity) and p-values, which indicate whether the smooths are significantly different from a flat line. Accordingly, the significant smooths indicate that target-over-competitor looks changed over time in both conditions, with the large effective degrees of freedom suggesting markedly non-linear timecourses.

The fixation curves predicted by the model are displayed in Figure 2A. In the match condition, target looks increase early on and keep increasing during the predictive window, whereas in the mismatch condition, the proportion of target looks remains at or below 50% for a longer period of time before it increases. To directly compare the two time smooths, we used the model with an ordered condition factor, as described above (Sóskuthy, 2017; Wieling, 2018; Wood, 2017). The results revealed that the difference smooth was statistically significant (χ 2 (7.23) = 28.46; p < .001), indicating that the two fixation curves differed in shape over time, and thus providing evidence for a distinct predictive timecourse in the two conditions.

Temporal onsets. Predictive effects were estimated to begin at 317 [146, 545] ms in the match condition and at 671 [609, 721] ms in the mismatch condition (see Fig. 2B for the full distributions of onsets). These estimates correspond to simple onsets, defined within each condition. To compare onset times between conditions, we obtained a distribution of onset differences by subtracting, for each simulation draw, the onset in the match condition from the corresponding onset in the mismatch condition. The comparison showed that the mismatch condition had a significantly later onset than the match condition (351 [87, 545] ms), consistent with the bootstrap-based results of Stone, Veríssimo, et al. (2021). As a robustness check, we repeated the onset estimation and between-condition comparison using four magnitude thresholds (0, 0.05, 0.1, and 0.15 log-odds; Appendix S1 in the target noun Supplementary Materials). Onsets were estimated to occur later as the magnitude threshold increased, but generally yielded the same conclusion as the default evidence-based criterion, with an earlier onset in the match than in the mismatch condition.

The predicted fixation curves in Figure 2A additionally showed that the mismatch condition exhibited a transient reversal of the target-over-competitor advantage, that is, a period with a smaller proportion of looks to the target than to the competitor image (around 250-700 ms). This suggests that the gender feature conveyed by the stem in the mismatch condition can facilitate looks to the competitor object, with which it matches (see Oltrogge et al., 2025; Stone, Veríssimo, et al., 2021, for discussion). The GAMM-based onset detection method can also be used to determine the onset of this reversal. To illustrate this, we ran an analysis in which an onset was defined as the first time point with a reliably smaller proportion of target-versus-competitor looks than at the baseline time. The onset of the target disadvantage in the mismatch condition was estimated at 304 [66, 468] ms, a similar time point to the onset of the predictive effect in the match condition.

Discussion

The results of our GAMM-based reanalysis of Stone, Veríssimo, et al. (2021) were largely consistent with their previous findings. Both the GAMM-based method proposed here and the bootstrap-based method showed that comprehenders predicted the target noun, and that this prediction had a distinct timecourse in the match versus mismatch conditions. Specifically, predictive effects arose earlier when the gender of the pronoun stem (which agrees with the possessor/antecedent) matched the gender of the target object, as compared to when it mismatched. As discussed by Stone, Veríssimo, et al. (2021), this suggests that the computation of coreference between the pronoun and its antecedent interfered with the prediction process, showing an interaction between antecedent retrieval and predictive processes.

There were also discrepancies between our results and those of Stone, Veríssimo, et al. (2021). Their window analysis revealed a larger predictive effect in the match than in the mismatch condition, but our analysis did not. This difference likely stems from the different statistical models that were fitted. Stone, Veríssimo, et al. (2021) employed a generalised mixed-effects model that did not include time as a predictor. In contrast, our GAMM analysis modelled fixation curves over time, with the model's parametric terms summarising overall target-looking across the whole analysis window. In this respect, the GAMM-based method provides a more comprehensive analysis, because it jointly characterises curve shape and derives onset times within a single model.

Another discrepancy between our results and those of Stone, Veríssimo, et al. (2021) was that the GAMM-based onset detection method produced earlier onset estimates than those of the bootstrap-based method (GAMM-based method: 317 ms and 671 ms for the match and mismatch conditions; bootstrap-based method: 402 ms and 709 ms). Moreover, the 95% intervals produced by the bootstrap-based method were narrower than those from the GAMM-based method, in the match condition (95% interval width of GAMMbased method: 399 ms; bootstrap-based method: 83 ms), the mismatch condition (112 ms vs. 34 ms) and their difference (458 ms vs. 90 ms).

Clearly, the two onset detection methods can yield different answers with regard to the timing and uncertainty of the estimated onsets. The GAMM-based method's ability to detect earlier effects suggests that it may have greater temporal sensitivity than the bootstrap-based method. Moreover, the fact that the bootstrap-based method produced narrower intervals suggests that it might underestimate the uncertainty around onsets. Before turning to a formal evaluation of the two methods (Study 3), we next apply the GAMM-based method to a second dataset that illustrates the estimation and comparison of difference curve onsets.

Study 2: Estimating and comparing divergences between conditions

In the previous section, the GAMM-based method was applied to an experimental design in which the central research question concerned estimating and comparing simple onsets, defined within each condition as the onset of a target-over-competitor advantage. In many cases, however, the key question cannot be answered by examining when a preference emerges within a single condition, but instead requires comparing fixation curves across conditions to determine when a predictor first has a detectable effect on the timecourse. In such situations, the relevant quantity is a difference curve onset, defined as the earliest time point at which the fixation curves in two different conditions begin to diverge.

A case in point is "target-absent designs", in which target and competitor objects do not co-exist within the same visual display (i.e., they are not presented within the same trial), but instead belong to different within-participant conditions. An example is a visual world study by Ito et al. (2018), which investigated the activation of target words and phonological competitors in L1 English speakers and L1 Japanese-L2 English speakers (for other examples of target-absent designs, see Huettig & Altmann, 2005; Rommers et al., 2013). Participants were presented with auditory sentences that contained a highly predictable word, such as cloud in The tourists expected rain when the sun went behind the cloud. In each trial, participants saw a four-object visual display, which appeared 1000 ms before the presentation of the target word. One of the four objects was the critical object. Depending on the experimental condition, the critical object was either the target word (an image of a cloud), a phonological competitor in English (an image of a clown, which shares its initial phonemes with cloud), a phonological competitor in Japanese (an image of a bear, because the Japanese word kuma 'bear' shares its first mora with kumo 'cloud'), or an unrelated image whose name did not share any phonological or semantic features with the target word (a globe). Only the critical object differed according to the experimental condition; the other three objects in the display (called "distractors") were held constant. Henceforth, we use the terms "target object", "English competitor", "Japanese competitor", and "unrelated object" to refer to the critical object shown in each condition, even though these objects were not presented together in the same display.

In such a design, the effects of interest are between-condition contrasts comparing looks to the target object, the English competitor, and the Japanese competitor against looks to the unrelated object. If participants pre-activated the target word cloud while hearing the sentence, we would expect more looks to the target object (the cloud) than to the unrelated object (the globe). Likewise, if participants pre-activated the phonological neighbours of the target, we would expect increased looks to the English competitor (the clown) relative to the unrelated object. For the L1 English group, the Japanese competitor served as a control: it was included to test phonological pre-activation in the L1 Japanese-L2 English group, but because the L1 participants did not speak Japanese, looks in this condition were expected to be similar to those in the unrelated condition.

We reanalysed the data from Ito et al.'s (2018) L1 group, which comprised 24 native English speakers who heard 16 experimental sentences (4 in each condition). Ito et al. (2018) analysed these data using growth-curve regression models and a sequential mixed-effects analysis in 50 ms bins. The sequential analysis showed that participants were more likely to look at the target object than at the unrelated object starting 400 ms after display onset. In addition, participants were more likely to look at the English competitor than at the unrelated object, but this effect was limited to a narrower time window between 500 and 650 ms. Ito and Knoeferle (2023) subsequently reanalysed this dataset using the bootstrap-based onset detection method of Stone, Lago, and Schad (2021). The divergence onset between looks to the target object and the unrelated object was estimated at 426 [350, 550] ms. Looks to the English competitor were not analysed with the bootstrap-based method, perhaps because this effect was confined to a relatively narrow time window in the original sequential analysis.

We applied the GAMM-based method to this dataset to obtain three complementary results: (a) a comparison of overall proportions of looks across conditions, (b) a timecourse analysis of fixation curves in each condition, and (c) estimates of difference curve onsets.

Methods

Following Ito and Knoeferle (2023), we analysed a time window that ranged from 200 ms after display onset (i.e., 800 ms before target-word onset) until 1000 ms after target-word onset. The initial 200 ms were excluded because the data contained very few valid observations. The dependent variable consisted of binomial counts of looks to the critical object (vs. looks to the three distractor objects in the display), aggregated for each participant × condition × 20 ms bin.

The GAMMs included a fixed effect of experimental condition (i.e., the identity of the critical object shown on a given trial) as a four-level, treatment-coded factor, with the unrelated condition as the reference level. Thus, in the parametric part of the model, the target object, English competitor, and Japanese competitor were each compared to the unrelated condition. The models additionally included a non-linear time smooth for each level of condition, each with the default basis dimension in mgcv (k = 10). As in Study 1, we fitted an additional GAMM with condition coded as an ordered factor to test timecourse differences relative to the unrelated condition.

As for the random-effects structure, models included random intercepts for participants and random slopes for condition, time, and their interaction, which were justified by significantly lower fREML scores (condition: χ 2 (3) = 773.67; p < .001; time: χ 2 (1) = 515.37; p < .001; condition-varying time slopes: χ 2 (3) = 1163.67; p < .001). We first fitted a non-autoregressive GAMM, which displayed a lag-1 residual autocorrelation of r = 0.87; we then refitted the model with an AR(1) error structure using this value.

Results

Overall proportions. The GAMM's parametric terms showed that participants looked more to the target object than to the unrelated object (b = 1.56; z = 7.68; p < .001) (condition was treatment-coded with the unrelated condition as the reference level, so the condition coefficients reflect differences relative to the unrelated object). Looks to the English competitor were also more frequent than looks to the unrelated object, but this difference was not statistically significant (b = 0.27; z = 1.57; p = .115). By contrast, looks to the Japanese competitor were very similar to those to the unrelated object (b = -0.01; z = -0.06; p = .951).

Note that these estimates summarise differences in target looking over the full analysis window on the modelled log-odds scale, including the 1000 ms period following the beginning of the target word. As a result, the greater proportion of looks to the target object reflects not only its predictive activation, but also the subsequent increase in looks after the target word is heard. To isolate predictive effects more specifically, the model would need to be fitted to a shorter window restricted to the 800 ms before the target word.

Timecourse of looking preferences. Table 2 summarises the model's smooth terms. The time smooths for the unrelated and Japanese competitor conditions were not statistically significant, providing no evidence that looks changed systematically over the analysis window in these conditions. By contrast, the time smooths for the target and English competitor conditions were significant, indicating that looks changed over time in these conditions (with their effective degrees of freedom indicating departures from linearity).

The fixation curves predicted by the model are displayed in Figure 3A. Consistent with the results for the smooth terms, the fixation curves in the unrelated and Japanese competitor conditions were relatively constant over time. Looks to the target object increased early and continued to rise during the predictive window (200-1000 ms), reaching 50-60% after the target word was heard. Finally, the fixation curves for the English competitor increased during the predictive window (until about 600 ms), but then decreased to values similar to those in the unrelated and Japanese competitor conditions. In the ordered factor model, the difference smooth for the target condition was statistically significant (χ 2 (3.56) = 14.97; p = .004), indicating that its timecourse differed from that of the unrelated condition. By contrast, the difference smooths for the English competitor (χ 2 (1.00) = 0.88; p = .348) and Japanese competitor conditions (χ 2 (1.00) = 0.00; p = .992) were not statistically significant.

Temporal onsets. The temporal onsets of interest were defined as the earliest point at which the GAMM-predicted fixation curves in the target, English competitor, and Japanese competitor conditions diverged from the fixation curve in the unrelated condition. To estimate difference curve onsets, we simulated difference curves directly from the fitted model (on the modelled log-odds scale), for each condition-minus-unrelated contrast. Onsets were then obtained from each simulated difference curve using the same baseline-corrected criterion as in Study 1: the first time point at which the difference between conditions was reliably greater than its predicted value at the baseline time (here, 200 ms after display onset).

Figure 3B shows the distributions of difference curve onsets for the target minus unrelated contrast (left panel) and the English competitor minus unrelated contrast (middle panel). Looks to the target object were estimated to diverge from the unrelated object at 280 [255, 324] ms, well before the auditory presentation of the target noun at 1000 ms. Looks to the English competitor diverged from the unrelated image slightly later, at 342 [273, 490] ms. Because both 95% HDIs were fully within the predictive window, the onset estimates suggest that activation of the target word (e.g., cloud) and of the phonological competitor (e.g., clown) occurred before the presentation of the target noun. The difference curve onsets for the target and English competitor contrasts (each relative to the unrelated condition) were directly compared by subtracting paired onset times across simulation draws (Fig. 3B, right panel). Looks to the target were estimated to diverge earlier than looks to the English competitor, but this comparison was not significant (-60 [-226, 25] ms).

We likewise repeated the onset estimation and comparison using the same four magnitude thresholds (Appendix S1 in the Supplementary Materials). Onset estimates occurred earlier than with the default evidence-based criterion, which likely reflects the high uncertainty of the model-predicted fixation curves given the relatively small sample size (24 participants and 4 sentences per participant per condition). Nevertheless, the substantive conclusion was generally unchanged: looks to the target tended to diverge earlier than looks to the English competitor, but there was not enough statistical evidence for a difference between their onsets.

Discussion

Our reanalysis of Ito et al.'s (2018) L1 data showed that looks to the target object diverged from looks to the unrelated object early on, around 250 to 300 ms after display onset, indicating that the target word was pre-activated by the sentence context. Similarly, looks to English phonological competitors diverged from those to unrelated objects within the predictive time window, suggesting that phonological neighbours of the target noun were likewise activated prior to the presentation of the target word. The predictive effect was estimated to occur earlier for the target object than for the English competitor, but the timecourse analyses and the direct comparison of their difference curve onsets provided limited statistical support. Importantly, this application also illustrates a feature of the GAMM-based method, namely, that it can estimate the timing of short-lived effects, such as looks to a phonological competitor (Ito, 2024). By contrast, the bootstrap-based method requires effects to be sustained for a minimum run time before they are detected, which may limit its sensitivity to such short-lived effects.

The results from the GAMM-based method were largely consistent with those reported by Ito and colleagues using a sequential mixed-effects analysis (Ito et al., 2018) and the bootstrap-based method (Ito & Knoeferle, 2023). However, one notable discrepancy was that the GAMM-based method produced earlier onsets than the other approaches (here, by about 100 to 150 ms), a pattern already observed in Study 1. This raises a natural question: which method more accurately estimates the underlying onset that gave rise to the data? Is the GAMM-based method detecting onsets too early, or is the bootstrap-based method detecting them too late? To address this question, we conducted two simulation studies in which the underlying fixation curves and their onset times were specified in advance, allowing us to compare the methods' ability to recover these values under controlled conditions.

Study 3: Evaluating the GAMM-based and bootstrap-based methods

This section formally evaluates the GAMM-based and bootstrap-based onset detection methods in two recovery simulations. Following previous studies of the same type (e.g., Aeschbach et al., 2024; Marra & Wood, 2012; Morris et al., 2019), the simulations were conducted as follows. First, we define the 'true' underlying parameter values of interest-in this case, target fixation curves and their temporal onsets. Second, we generate multiple synthetic datasets from these curves. Third, we apply the two onset detection methods to each dataset to estimate the underlying parameters. Finally, we assess each method's ability to recover the specified values using multiple performance measures (outlined below). We compared the performance of the GAMM-based and bootstrap-based methods in a range of controlled scenarios, in which we varied the type of effect being detected (simple onsets, comparisons of simple onsets, and difference curve onsets), the shape of the underlying fixation curves, the number of participants and items, and the level of random noise.

Method

Generation of underlying fixation curves.

We conducted two simulation studies, each featuring two within-participant conditions. Each condition was associated with an underlying fixation curve and a corresponding temporal onset. Simulation 1 was designed to evaluate the ability of the GAMM-based and bootstrap-based methods to detect an earlier (simple) onset, a later (simple) onset, and their comparison (see Fig. 4, top panel). This type of experimental design mirrors studies such as Stone, Veríssimo, et al. (2021), in which the question of interest was whether predictive effects arose earlier in one condition than the other (see Study 1).

The underlying fixation curves were generated by the following quadratic polynomial functions:

We chose to use quadratic polynomials (on the log-odds scale) as the underlying fixation curves because they capture some of the essential characteristics of target-versuscompetitor looks, namely, that looks to the target image remain at or below chance level during an initial time period and then gradually increase as the target preference builds up. This is a pattern commonly obtained in visual world prediction studies (e.g., Dussias et al., 2013; Huettig & Janse, 2016) and one that resembles the data presented in our Study 1 above (particularly in the mismatch condition, Stone, Veríssimo, et al., 2021). Other similar functions were also considered (e.g., the 4-parameter logistic, McMurray et al., 2010), but the quadratic had the advantage of yielding not only a gradual build-up of target looks, but also a well-defined onset (see next paragraph for onset definitions). However, our assumed fixation curves should be regarded only as useful idealisations; they were not intended to strictly replicate the fixation curves observed in visual world studies, which can follow different kinds of functions (e.g., McMurray, 2023; Mirman, 2014).

The fixation curves in Simulation 1 crossed the 50% baseline at exactly 500 ms in the earlier-onset condition and 750 ms in the later-onset condition. We therefore took these crossing points as the 'true' underlying onset values, yielding an onset difference of 250 ms (see Fig. 4). Although the GAMM-based and bootstrap-based methods use different onset detection criteria, we evaluated them against the same underlying onsets and onset difference. Specifically, in the GAMM-based method, an onset is estimated as the earliest time point at which the modelled fixation curve reliably surpasses its value at baseline (i.e., its predicted value at 𝑡 0 ). In contrast, in the bootstrap-based method, an onset is estimated as the earliest time point at which the proportion of target looks significantly exceeds 50%. Since the underlying fixation curves were both at 50% at 𝑡 0 by construction, the same onset values were used to evaluate both methods, despite their different operational criteria.

In Simulation 2, the fixation curves were generated by the following quadratic functions (Fig. 4, bottom panel):

Simulation 2 differed from Simulation 1 in three respects. First, both conditions had an onset at 500 ms, so that their onset difference was 0 ms. This allowed us to assess the extent to which the methods appropriately identified a null difference between conditions. Second, although the onsets were identical in the two conditions, their fixation curves differed. One condition showed a more gradual or 'shallower' increase in target looks over time, while the other condition showed a more pronounced or 'steeper' increase. By comparing the two conditions, we could evaluate whether the steepness of the increase influenced the methods' performance, for example, by enhancing their ability to detect an onset. Third, Simulation 2 included a divergence between conditions, defined as the time point at which looks in the steeper-onset condition first exceed those in the shallower-onset condition. In our method, this divergence is detected as a difference curve onset. This design mirrors studies like Ito et al. (2018), in which the effects of interest depend on a comparison between the fixation curves corresponding to two conditions (see Study 2). As was the case for the simple onsets, the divergence occurred at 500 ms (see Fig. 4, bottom panel).

Simulation of synthetic data. We assessed the influence of two design variables on the methods' performance: sample size (small, medium, large) and noise level (high, medium, low). These variables were crossed to create nine different scenarios intended to reflect the typical characteristics of visual world studies in psycholinguistics.

The sample size configurations were defined by varying the numbers of participants and items simultaneously. The small-sample datasets included simulated data from 20 participants × 10 items, the medium-sample datasets were based on 50 participants × 25 onset 1: 500ms onset 2: 750 ms

Simulation 1 0 250 500 750 1000 1250 1500 30% 40% 50% 60% 70% 80% 90% 100% Time [ms] Underlying proportions of looks to target onset 1: 500ms onset 2: 500 ms onset of divergence: 500ms Simulation 2 0 250 500 750 1000 1250 1500 30% 40% 50% 60% 70% 80% 90% 100% Time [ms] Underlying proportions of looks to target items, and the large-sample datasets used 80 participants × 40 items. These numbers were chosen to reflect the fact that visual world experiments typically test more participants than items. For simplicity, each participant was assumed to see every item in both conditions, so that the number of items equalled the number of trials per participant and condition; no item variability was simulated.

The noise levels consisted of three different amounts of inter-individual variation, which were expressed as different random-effect standard deviations (SDs) in the modelled log-odds scale. Datasets in the high-noise scenarios were generated assuming a random intercept SD of 0.4 and a random slope SD of 0.8; the medium-noise scenarios had random SDs of 0.25 and 0.5; and the low-noise scenarios had random SDs of 0.1 and 0.2. For simplicity, we assumed inter-individual variation only in the linear effects of time, not the quadratic effects. Random intercepts were assumed to vary less than random slopes, because random intercepts capture the variation in proportions of looks at the beginning of the time window, which is expected to be relatively small in a well-matched experiment. In contrast, random slopes reflect variation in the steepness of fixation curves over time, which can depend on various participant characteristics (e.g., Huettig et al., 2011; Ribu et al., 2024). We additionally ensured that the selected random-effect SDs were similar to those obtained in real psycholinguistic experiments by analysing Stone, Veríssimo, et al.'s (2021) data reported in Study 1. A quadratic model fitted to this dataset showed random-effect SDs between our medium and high noise levels (intercept: 0.30; slope: 0.65), while a GAMM with an autocorrelation term produced smaller values (intercept: 0.02; slope: 0.35).

We generated 5,000 synthetic datasets in each of the nine design scenarios, according to the following steps. First, for each participant, we sampled a random intercept and a random slope from independent normal distributions with a mean of 0 and an SD determined by the corresponding noise level; these random effects were shared across the two conditions. Second, the simulated random effects were added to the fixed intercept and slope in the equations above to generate participant-specific fixation curves over time. Third, we simulated counts of looks to the target image, for each participant and condition at every 20 ms interval. The counts were sampled from binomial distributions with two parameters: an underlying proportion, which was given by the participant-specific fixation curves at a particular time point, and a total number of looks, which was equal to the assumed number of trials for a given sample size scenario. Thus, the synthetic data mirrored the format of the real data used in Studies 1 and 2 above, with looks binned at 20 ms intervals and aggregated over trials.

We note that the synthetic looks were generated by sampling independently at each time bin. In other words, at every 20 ms there was a separate "roll of the dice" that generated the observed counts. This sampling scheme is known to be inconsistent with how eye movements are generated, since it does not take into account the serial nature of discrete fixations (McMurray, 2023). We therefore treat these simulations as an initial benchmark, and return to this limitation in the General Discussion.

Evaluation of the methods' performance.

The methods were applied to synthetic datasets generated as above, with 5,000 datasets per method and scenario. For the GAMMbased method, we fitted a binomial GAMM with a time smooth for each condition and by-participant random intercepts and random slopes for time. No autocorrelation term was included, since the synthetic looks were generated independently at each time bin. Onsets were estimated with the same criterion as in Studies 1 and 2, using 10,000 posterior simulations. For the bootstrap-based method, which is computationally more costly, we used 2,500 bootstrap iterations (Stone, Lago, & Schad, 2021, used 2,000, and considered 1,000-2,000 iterations to be sufficient). As in the original method, in each iteration, looks were resampled with replacement within each participant, condition, and time bin. A onesample t-test against 50% was conducted at each bin, and an onset was defined as the first of at least 200 ms of consecutive significant bins. Difference curve onsets were estimated analogously, using paired t-tests between conditions.

Performance was assessed using multiple measures in each sample size and noise level combination. Some of the most commonly used performance measures in simulation studies are bias, variance, root mean squared error, and CI coverage (Morris et al., 2019; White et al., 2024). Each of these measures quantifies how well a statistical method can recover the underlying values from which the data were generated. Because Study 3 was a formal assessment of the methods, the onset distributions produced by both methods were summarised using means and quantile-based CIs, in line with the definitions of bias and interval coverage used in the simulations. By contrast, Studies 1 and 2 report medians and HDIs, as recommended above for empirical applications.

A method's bias is computed as the difference between the mean of its estimates and the underlying value. A method is unbiased if the mean of its estimates across simulated datasets is identical to this value. If the average estimate overshoots or undershoots the underlying value, a method is said to have positive or negative bias, respectively.

A method's variance captures the extent to which its estimates vary across simulated datasets. If a method has high variance, its estimates vary more widely around their mean. If a method has low variance, it consistently produces similar estimates across simulations. We assessed the variability of the estimates using their standard deviation (SD) across simulations (also called the 'empirical standard error'); additionally, we calculated the average width of the 95% CIs as a measure of the uncertainty reported by each method (Morris et al., 2019; White et al., 2024). Ideally, a method should display both low bias and low variance, that is, its estimates should cluster around the underlying value and vary little. However, reducing bias can come at the cost of increased variability (Geman et al., 1992; James et al., 2021), making it important to evaluate these properties together (Morris et al., 2019; White & Royston, 2009).

To assess the combined effects of bias and variability, we also calculated the root mean squared error (RMSE), defined as the square root of the mean squared difference between the estimates and the underlying value across simulated datasets (Morris et al., 2019). RMSE provides a measure of overall estimation accuracy, with lower values indicating more accurate recovery of the underlying value.

Another key performance measure is CI coverage. Like bias, coverage has a clearly defined target: for a given significance level 𝛼, a method's CIs should contain the underlying value in 100 × (1 -𝛼)% of repeated samples (Neyman, 1934). For example, the method's 95% CIs should include the underlying value in 95% of the conducted simulations; the method's 90% CIs should include the underlying value in 90% of the simulations, etc. In the context of the current simulation study, CI coverage is of particular interest, because one of the main advantages of the bootstrap-based method of Stone, Lago, and Schad (2021) and the current GAMM-based method (relative to other analytical methods for visual world) is that they allow researchers to determine CIs around temporal estimates.

We also calculated bias-adjusted coverage as a diagnostic measure that assesses the contribution of systematic bias to CI coverage. For each method, effect, and simulation scenario, we subtracted the empirical bias (i.e., the mean estimate minus the underlying value) from the onset estimates and their CI bounds, and then recalculated coverage. This adjustment preserves the dispersion of estimates across simulations and their CI widths, allowing us to evaluate coverage independently of systematic bias.

Finally, if a method can be used to test a null hypothesis (𝐻 0 ), its performance can also be assessed by calculating rates of 𝐻 0 rejection. The bootstrap-based method and the GAMMbased method can both be used to perform hypothesis tests. For example, the comparison of onset times in the match and mismatch conditions in Study 1 constituted a null hypothesis test, with statistical significance determined by whether the 95% interval of the difference distribution excluded zero. When 𝐻 0 is false, rates of rejection indicate statistical power; when 𝐻 0 is true, rates of rejection constitute Type I error rates. An ideal hypothesis-testing method should reject only 100 × 𝛼% of true null hypotheses (the nominal rate of Type I errors) and as many false null hypotheses as possible (i.e., it should have high power). The current simulations allowed us to determine both power and Type I error rates, because in Simulation 1 the underlying onsets were different (i.e., 𝐻 0 is false), and in Simulation 2 the underlying onsets were equal (i.e., 𝐻 0 is true) (see Fig. 4). Thus, the proportion of 95% CIs that excluded zero (indicating a significant difference) was equal to power in Simulation 1 and to the rate of Type I errors in Simulation 2.

Results of Simulation 1

Bias. Figure 5 displays the mean estimates of onset 1 (earlier), onset 2 (later), and their difference (i.e., the comparison between the two onsets), for both the GAMM-based and bootstrap-based methods, in the different sample size and noise level scenarios. The bias of each method is the difference between the means and the underlying values (which are represented by the dashed lines in Fig. 5).

The GAMM-based method showed relatively small bias overall, although the bias of simple onset estimates varied systematically with sample size and noise level. Estimates of the simple onsets were later than their underlying values, with bias decreasing as sample size increased and increasing with higher noise. Across the two simple onsets, bias ranged from 9 to 20 ms under low noise, 25-47 ms under medium noise, and 42-82 ms under high noise. Estimates of the difference between onsets were especially accurate, remaining within 6 ms of the underlying value of 250 ms in every scenario.

The bootstrap-based method exhibited much larger bias than the GAMM-based method in every scenario, but the extent of this disadvantage depended on several factors. The bootstrap-based estimates of simple onsets were particularly inaccurate, revealing delays of 152-231 ms at the smallest sample size, 67-119 ms for medium-sized samples, and 46-87 ms for the largest sample size. Thus, for the estimation of simple onsets, smaller sample sizes consistently generated more biased onset estimates. However, the bootstrap method's estimate of the comparison between onsets was much less biased, undershooting the underlying value by 40-45 ms at the smallest sample size, 21-25 ms at the medium sample size, and 15-16 ms at the largest sample size. This suggests that the bootstrap-based method performed considerably better when estimating a difference between two onsets, which was the specific scenario considered in the study that proposed it (Stone, Lago, & Schad, 2021).

Variance. We calculated the SDs of estimates across simulations as a measure of each method's variability (the SDs are shown as error bars in Fig. 5). Across all effects and scenarios, SDs ranged from 10 to 60 ms for the GAMM-based method and 10-49 ms for the bootstrap-based method. The GAMM-based estimates were somewhat more variable at the smallest sample size, but the variability of the two methods was similar at medium and large sample sizes. For both methods, variability decreased substantially with increasing sample size. For the simple onsets, higher random noise was also generally associated with greater variability.

As an additional measure of uncertainty, we calculated the average width of the 95% CIs (Appendix S2 in the Supplementary Materials). Across scenarios, average CI widths ranged between 39 and 265 ms for the GAMM-based method and between 38 and 189 ms for the bootstrap-based method. GAMM-based intervals were generally wider for the simple onsets, whereas the relative width of the intervals for the onset comparison depended on sample size. We consider the implications of these differences together with CI coverage below.

Root mean squared error. The GAMM-based method showed substantially lower RMSE than the bootstrap-based method for both simple onsets across all nine scenarios (GAMM-based: 14-102 ms; bootstrap-based: 47-235 ms). For the onset comparison, the GAMM-based method also had lower RMSE at medium (GAMM-based: 22-23 ms; bootstrap-based: 27-29 ms) and large sample sizes (GAMM-based: 15 ms; bootstrap-based: 19-20 ms). At the smallest sample size, the two methods performed similarly (GAMM-based: 48-58 ms; bootstrap-based: 48-52 ms). In sum, when considering bias and variability together, the GAMM-based method generally provided more accurate onset estimates (see Appendix S3 in the Supplementary Materials).

Coverage. The empirical coverage of the 90%, 95%, and 99% CIs is shown in Figure 6 for the GAMM-based method and Figure 7 for the bootstrap-based method. Summaries of the empirical coverage in the different scenarios are shown in Table 3. For the GAMM-based method, coverage of the simple onsets was below the nominal level and varied systematically across noise and sample size conditions. For the 95% CIs, coverage of the two simple onsets was relatively high under low noise (88%-92%), but decreased under medium noise (67%-81%) and high noise (54%-69%). Coverage also tended to decrease with increasing sample size. By contrast, coverage of the onset comparison was very close to the nominal level in every scenario, ranging from 95% to 96%.

The bootstrap-based method showed substantially poorer coverage of the simple onsets in every scenario: only 0%-4% of the 95% CIs contained the underlying onset values. However, coverage of the onset comparison was satisfactory, ranging from 93% to 97%. Thus, although the GAMM-based method did not achieve nominal coverage for the simple onsets, its coverage was substantially higher than that of the bootstrap-based method across all scenarios, while both methods showed approximately nominal coverage for the onset comparison.

We next examined whether the observed undercoverage was primarily attributable to systematic bias in the onset estimates or to confidence intervals that were too narrow. To this end, we recalculated coverage after subtracting each method's empirical bias from its estimates and CI bounds (Table 3). For the GAMM-based method, bias-adjusted 95% coverage was close to the nominal 95% level across all effects and scenarios (94%-96%), suggesting that its undercoverage was due to delayed onset estimates. For the bootstrap-based method, bias-adjusted coverage of the simple onsets remained much more variable (52%-98%), whereas coverage of the onset comparison became conservative (98%-100%). Thus, for the bootstrap-based method, undercoverage of the simple onsets reflected both bias (see above) and, in many scenarios, confidence intervals that were too narrow.

Power. The statistical power of both methods is shown in Figure 8. Both methods had very high power to detect the underlying 250 ms difference between onsets across all sample size and noise scenarios. For the GAMM-based method, power ranged from 99.5% to 99.9% at the smallest sample size and reached 100% at the medium and large sample sizes.

Results of Simulation 2

Bias. Figure 9 displays the means and SDs of the estimates produced by the GAMMbased and bootstrap-based methods. The GAMM-based method showed relatively small bias overall, although the amount of bias differed across effects. Estimates of simple onsets were on average later than their underlying values, with bias decreasing as sample size increased and increasing with higher noise. Bias was larger for onset 1 (shallower; 11-82 ms) than for onset 2 (steeper; 5-43 ms). Estimates of the comparison between onsets undershot zero by 3-39 ms. Estimates of the divergence between conditions were especially accurate, with very small bias (11-18 ms) across all scenarios. The results are presented for onset 1 (shallower), onset 2 (steeper), the onset comparison, and the divergence between conditions, in each of the nine scenarios defined by crossing sample sizes (number of participants × items) with random noise levels (high, medium, low). Dashed lines mark the underlying values of onset 1, onset 2, their comparison, and the divergence.
