Note.

Values indicate the minimum-maximum coverage across sample sizes and noise levels. Unadjusted coverage is the empirical coverage of the intervals returned by each method. For bias-adjusted coverage, estimates were shifted to remove their empirical bias within each scenario, while preserving their dispersion and confidence interval widths, and coverage was then recomputed relative to the underlying value.

As in Simulation 1, we also examined coverage after adjusting for empirical bias (Table 3). For the GAMM-based method, bias-adjusted 95% coverage was close to the nominal level across all effects and scenarios (93%-96%). For the bootstrap-based method, bias-adjusted coverage remained more variable for the simple onsets (61%-98%) and the onset comparison (90%-100%), whereas coverage of the divergence increased to 95%-99%. Thus, the undercoverage of the GAMM-based method was again primarily attributable to bias in the estimates, whereas for the bootstrap-based method, bias did not fully account for the undercoverage of the simple onsets and, in some scenarios, the onset comparison. Type I error rates. Type I error rates for the comparison between onsets were computed for each method as the proportion of their 95% CIs that excluded zero (see Fig. 8). Note that since the underlying difference between onsets was zero, Type I error rates are equal to 1 minus the empirical coverage of the 95% CIs (discussed above). For the GAMM-based method, Type I error rates were close to the nominal 5% rate under low noise scenarios, but increased for medium and high noise (reaching 26% at its maximum). The bootstrap-based method showed considerably higher Type I error rates than the GAMM-based method, ranging from 10% to 65% across scenarios. Thus, both methods sometimes detected spurious differences between onsets, although this occurred less often with the GAMM-based method.

Discussion

Across the two simulation studies, the GAMM-based method produced substantially less biased estimates than the bootstrap-based method. This was the case for simple onsets, onset comparisons, and the divergence between conditions. The variability of estimates was broadly similar between the two methods, although GAMM-based estimates were more variable at the smallest sample size. Considering bias and variability together, the GAMM-based method generally provided more accurate estimates, as indicated by its lower RMSE.

For simple onsets, both methods tended to produce estimates that were later than their generating values, and these systematic delays contributed to undercoverage of the underlying onsets. However, the delays were considerably smaller for the GAMM-based method, which also showed markedly higher raw coverage of the simple onsets. After adjusting the estimates for their empirical bias, coverage of the GAMM-based intervals was close to nominal across all effects and scenarios. This indicates that their widths adequately represented the variability of the estimates across simulated datasets, with the undercoverage primarily resulting from systematic bias. For the bootstrap-based method, bias adjustment increased coverage substantially, but undercoverage of simple onsets remained in many scenarios. Thus, the poor coverage of the bootstrap-based method reflected not only systematic delays in the onset estimates, but also confidence intervals that were often too narrow.

An apparently counterintuitive finding was that unadjusted GAMM-based coverage of the simple onsets tended to decrease with increasing sample size, particularly under higher noise, even though the estimates became less biased. This pattern can be understood by considering the remaining bias relative to the width of the confidence intervals. Larger samples brought the estimates closer to the underlying onset values, but also reduced their variability and narrowed their intervals. The remaining bias therefore became more consequential relative to interval width, so that better accuracy did not necessarily translate into better coverage. The approximately nominal coverage obtained after bias adjustment across all sample sizes supports this interpretation.

Turning to onset comparisons, both methods performed relatively well in Simulation 1, showing considerably less bias than for the individual onsets, approximately nominal coverage, and very high power to detect the underlying onset difference. The relatively low bias was due to the two simple onsets being delayed by similar amounts within each method, so that their difference remained close to the underlying value. The GAMM-based method was particularly accurate, but the bootstrap-based method also performed well in a scenario similar to that originally examined by Stone, Lago, and Schad (2021) when proposing the method.

However, Simulation 2 showed that onset comparisons can become biased when the shapes of the underlying fixation curves differ. Although the two conditions had the same generating onset, the shallower effect was estimated as occurring later than the steeper effect. Their comparison was therefore biased away from zero, leading to undercoverage and inflated Type I error rates. This occurred for both methods, although it was considerably more pronounced for the bootstrap-based method. Thus, comparisons between estimated onsets can be affected when conditions differ in how rapidly their effects emerge, even when their generating onsets are identical.

General Discussion

This article introduced a method based on generalised additive mixed models (GAMMs) to detect onsets of experimental effects in visual world eye-tracking data. Characterising the temporal properties of experimental effects, such as their onset or offset, is critical for evaluating psycholinguistic processing theories, for example, in debates about the timecourse of semantic versus morphosyntactic computations (Reichle, 2021; Staub, 2015; Sturt, 2003), the onset and/or speed of linguistic predictions (Huettig et al., 2022; Pickering & Gambi, 2018), and the potential differences between populations, such as ageing individuals and bilingual speakers (e.g., L. B. Fernandez et al., 2025; Ito et al., 2018; Lago et al., 2023; Vanek et al., 2024). Given the relevance of these issues, different methods have been used to estimate and compare the onsets (or offsets) of experimental effects in the visual world paradigm (Ito et al., 2018; McMurray, Aslin, et al., 2008; Salverda et al., 2014). One increasingly adopted approach is the bootstrap-based onset detection method proposed by Stone, Lago, and Schad (2021). Although recent work has evaluated its Type I error rate when comparing latencies between groups (Minor, 2026), its accuracy in recovering underlying onset values has not been formally assessed. Our study addressed this gap by evaluating the bootstrap-based method alongside our newly proposed GAMM-based method.

The GAMM-based method involves fitting a GAMM, simulating multiple fixation curves from the fitted model, calculating an onset for each simulated curve, and obtaining a distribution of temporal onsets, which can then be compared between conditions or participant groups. To demonstrate the applicability of the method, we reanalysed two studies that illustrate two common experimental designs used in the visual world literature. The first study, conducted by Stone, Veríssimo, et al. (2021), examined morphosyntactic predictions in sentences where a syntactically irrelevant dependency either matched or mismatched the predictive gender cue. Our analysis demonstrated that the GAMM-based method could be used to (a) estimate the time point at which a target-over-competitor preference first emerged in each condition, and (b) compare prediction onsets between conditions to show a significantly earlier predictive effect in one condition than in the other. The second study, conducted by Ito et al. (2018), employed a target-absent design to examine how sentence contexts activated predictable target words and their phonological competitors. In this design, the effects of interest depended on a comparison between fixation curves in different conditions. Because GAMMs can compute (and simulate data from) difference curves, the onset detection method was able to estimate those divergence points, and to reveal the timing of predictive effects for both predictable target words and their phonological neighbours. Both of our reanalyses were broadly consistent with the findings reported by Ito et al. (2018) and Stone, Veríssimo, et al. (2021). However, the GAMM-based method estimated earlier onset times than the bootstrap-based onset detection method proposed by Stone, Lago, and Schad (2021).

In addition to demonstrating the applicability of the GAMM-based method to typical visual world paradigms, we formally assessed its performance and compared it with that of the bootstrap-based method in two simulations. The GAMM-based method produced onset estimates that were substantially less biased than those of the bootstrap-based method. This advantage was also reflected in generally lower RMSE, indicating that, when bias and variability were considered together, the GAMM-based method provided more accurate estimates of the underlying onset values. However, both methods tended to estimate simple onsets and divergences that were later than the underlying onset times from which the data were generated. Although the GAMM-based method brought the estimates closer to those values, a systematic delay remained.

Why do both methods tend to produce delayed estimates? An explanation follows from the distinction between the underlying onset of an effect and the evidence required to detect it. In our simulations, the underlying simple onsets were defined as the exact times at which the generating curves crossed the 50% baseline, or, in the case of difference curve onsets, when the steeper curve crossed above the shallower curve. However, both methods define an onset as the earliest point in time at which an effect is reliably found, that is, when the estimated effect is sufficiently large relative to its uncertainty. Satisfying this criterion generally requires a further increase beyond the underlying crossing point, and hence, additional time. The delay depends on how rapidly the effect increases and how precisely it is estimated. For both methods, a shallower increase or greater uncertainty can postpone detection, even when the underlying crossing point remains unchanged.

A natural question is whether these delays could be avoided by using a fixed magnitude criterion, as examined in Studies 1 and 2. However, a gradually increasing effect still needs time to reach a positive threshold, even when that threshold is independent of statistical precision (cf. J. Miller et al., 1998; Ulrich & Miller, 2001). Our magnitude threshold analyses illustrated this directly, since onset estimates occurred progressively later as the threshold increased (Appendix S1 in the Supplementary Materials), a pattern also observed in ERP and visual world analyses that used multiple percent-of-maximum thresholds (McMurray, Aslin, et al., 2008; J. Miller et al., 1998; Ulrich & Miller, 2001). The choice of threshold can therefore affect the extent of the detection delay, but does not eliminate it. Some separation between an underlying onset and a detected onset is inherent whenever 'onset' is operationalised by requiring an effect to reach a criterion, whether that criterion is defined in terms of statistical evidence or effect magnitude.

One might instead consider setting the threshold to zero, so that an onset is detected as soon as a curve exceeds the comparison value by any amount. Unfortunately, this would allow arbitrarily small changes to determine onset estimates. In practice, fixation curves (both observed and simulated) can contain small fluctuations around baseline, allowing transient increases early in the analysis window to determine the estimated onset even when the main increase of interest occurs much later. This behaviour was apparent in our sensitivity analyses: with a threshold of zero, onset distributions extended to the very beginning of the analysis window in Study 1 and were concentrated at its lower boundary in Study 2 (Appendix S1 in the Supplementary Materials). Thus, lowering the threshold to zero increases sensitivity to these fluctuations without necessarily improving recovery of the underlying onset. A positive magnitude criterion guards against such fluctuations by requiring a minimum effect size, whereas our evidence-based criterion serves a similar purpose by requiring the departure to be sufficiently large relative to the modelled uncertainty.

Besides showing lower bias, the GAMM-based method generally showed substantially better CI coverage than the bootstrap-based method, although its coverage was still often below nominal levels. A further diagnostic analysis showed that, after removing empirical bias while preserving the dispersion of the estimates and their CI widths, GAMM-based 95% coverage was approximately nominal across all effects and scenarios (Table 3). These results suggest that the GAMM-based intervals adequately represented sampling variability, with undercoverage of its CIs being primarily attributable to the onset delays. By contrast, the bootstrap-based intervals continued to show undercoverage in several scenarios even after bias adjustment, indicating additional limitations in this method's quantification of uncertainty. We emphasise, however, that this adjustment served only a diagnostic purpose; it cannot be applied directly to empirical datasets, where the underlying onset values are unknown.

An important question is whether detection delays also affect comparisons between onsets, which are often the main motivation for onset analyses. Our simulations suggest that if the two onsets are delayed by similar amounts, the difference between them can still be appropriately estimated. This was the pattern in Simulation 1, where both methods showed approximately nominal coverage and very high power for the onset comparison, despite delaying individual estimates. However, Simulation 2 showed that onset comparisons can become biased and Type I error rates can be inflated when fixation curves differ in steepness. Specifically, although the two conditions had the same underlying onset, the shallower curve took longer to satisfy the detection criterion than the steeper curve. The resulting difference in delays led both methods to detect significant onset differences even though they had the same underlying onset. These spurious differences were nevertheless less frequent for the GAMM-based method, with Type I error rates ranging from the nominal 5% rate under low noise scenarios up to 26%, compared to 10% to 65% for the bootstrap-based method.

Although these results favour the GAMM-based method, they also highlight the need for caution when interpreting onset comparisons. Researchers cannot ensure that conditions or groups will be similarly biased, particularly because they do not possess a benchmark for what should count as "similar steepness" 2 . Moreover, our simulations showed that variations in sample size and noise levels-not only steepness-can modulate the bias of both methods. Accordingly, if two conditions or groups differ in sample size or variability, their onset comparison might also be biased, potentially inflating Type I error rates. Although we did not directly evaluate such differences, this possibility is particularly relevant when comparing participant populations that may differ in variability (e.g., L. B. Fernandez et al., 2025; Hua et al., 2025; Nguyen & Grüter, 2024; Stone, Lago, & Schad, 2021; Vanek et al., 2024). This reinforces the need to interpret onset comparisons as differences in the time at which the specified onset criterion is met. This may reflect not only differences in the underlying onset times, but also differences in the additional time required for each effect to meet that criterion.

Given that the GAMM-based method showed advantages in recovering the underlying onset values, with substantially smaller bias, lower RMSE, and better CI coverage than those of the bootstrap-based method, we recommend that researchers adopt the GAMMbased approach. To support this transition, we have developed an R package (available at https://gitlab.com/jlverissimo/onsets) that implements the GAMM-based method and makes it straightforward to estimate and compare onsets for different conditions or groups.

Advantages of the GAMM-based method

Beyond providing more accurate onset estimates and generally better CI coverage, the GAMM-based method offers several advantages over the bootstrap-based method. First, it leverages the strengths of GAMMs for modelling timeseries data, including the ability to fit non-linear shapes without requiring researchers to commit to a specific functional form. In addition, GAMMs use penalisation to discourage excessive wiggliness, which helps control overfitting in a principled way. This contrasts with other approaches that are often applied to visual world data, such as growth-curve models (e.g., Ito et al., 2018; Mirman, 2014), parametric non-linear curve-fitting (e.g., Farris-Trimble & McMurray, 2013; McMurray et al., 2010), and BDOTS (Seedorff et al., 2018), which require assumptions about the shape of the timecourse and can therefore be more vulnerable to under-or overfitting when those assumptions are misspecified.

Other key advantages of the GAMM-based method stem from its foundation as a statistical model of fixation curves over time. Unlike the bootstrap-based method (Stone, Lago, & Schad, 2021) and threshold-jackknifing approaches (e.g., McMurray, Aslin, et al., 2008; Reinisch & Sjerps, 2013), our approach seamlessly integrates curve fitting and onset detection within a single framework: we first fit a model that accounts for looking preferences over time, and then derive onset estimates from the model-predicted fixation curves. Because onset estimation is based on model predictions rather than on the observed data, the approach naturally smooths out any irregularities in the observed data, which reduces the risk of overfitting. In addition, a model-based approach allows researchers to incorporate additional predictors into their GAMMs to obtain the best model for their data, for example, adding fixed or random effects to control for confounds and account for variability across participants. Finally, whereas other onset detection approaches typically require separate analyses to establish whether an effect is present and to characterise its timecourse, the GAMM-based approach provides a unified analysis of looking proportions, timecourse dynamics, and onsets of experimental effects, ensuring that inference about these different aspects remains internally consistent.

A final advantage of the GAMM-based method relative to the bootstrap-based method is its computational efficiency. GAMMs benefit from a number of features that speed up computation (Wieling, 2018), and can therefore be fitted quickly when using aggregated data as in the present analyses (the models reported in this paper were fitted in under one second on a modern laptop computer). Moreover, the GAMM-based method requires fitting only one statistical model, from which the simulated curves are obtained. This enables researchers to fit more complex statistical models, for example, with additional covariates or larger random-effects structures. By comparison, the bootstrap-based method requires fitting a statistical model to every bootstrapped dataset, which restricts the complexity of models that can be fitted in a reasonable amount of time. For this reason, the bootstrap-based method is commonly implemented with a t-test on proportions, which may not be the most suitable modelling choice (Stone, Lago, & Schad, 2021; Veríssimo & Clahsen, 2014).

At the same time, our method preserves a key benefit of the bootstrap-based method, namely that it returns full distributions of onset estimates. This means that researchers are not restricted to a particular set of contrasts, but can carry out further comparisons of interest by operating directly on onset samples. For instance, if a researcher wished to test whether an onset comparison (e.g., between two conditions, such as match vs. mismatch, Stone, Veríssimo, et al., 2021) itself differed across two participant groups (e.g., two L2 groups with different L1 backgrounds, Lago et al., 2023), the procedure would be straightforward: first obtain a distribution of the comparison between two onsets (mismatch minus match) within each group, then subtract these two distributions sample-wise to obtain a distribution of the interaction effect (i.e., a difference of differences). As above, if the 95% HDI of the resulting distribution excluded zero, this would provide evidence that the condition effect on onset timing differed between groups. Thus, our GAMM-based method is not limited to the simple contrasts reported in the present paper, but can be flexibly extended to more complex experimental designs.

Limitations of the GAMM-based method

One limitation of the GAMM models used in this article is that they were fitted to data binned in 20 ms intervals and aggregated by participant. Aggregating by participant prevents the inclusion of random effects by item. As a result, the models we used do not account for systematic variability across sentences or pictures, which can lead to an underestimation of variability in the data (Barr et al., 2013; Veríssimo, 2023). We used participant-aggregated data for several reasons. First, GAMMs fitted to trial-level visual world data can yield residuals with extremely high autocorrelation (often over 0.99), which is difficult to model appropriately in a subsequent autoregressive GAMM. A further option would have been to use larger time bins (e.g., 50 ms or 100 ms, Stone, Lago, & Schad, 2021), but this would have reduced temporal resolution and could have obscured subtle changes in the timecourse of looks. Second, we opted for more parsimonious models to reduce overfitting and preserve statistical power (Bates et al., 2018). In the specific case of GAMMs, maximal models that include all random effects allowed by the design have been described as "ill-advised", due to the risk of over-parametrisation and uninterpretable parameters (Baayen et al., 2017). Finally, simpler models can be fitted (and simulated from) much more efficiently than models fitted on trial-level data.

Our strategy of using 20 ms bins, participant-aggregated data, and autocorrelation modelling represents a compromise, aimed at balancing temporal resolution with adequate management of autocorrelation within the GAMM framework. However, other choices would be possible, for example, using larger time bins to reduce autocorrelation, analysing triallevel data, or even aggregating by item to investigate the effect of by-item predictors. We do not yet know how these choices affect the performance of the GAMM-based method, nor how they affect other analytic methods for visual world data (although recent work has begun to evaluate the effect of some of these analytical choices on the bootstrap-based method, L. Fernandez et al., 2026). To establish clearer guidelines for data processing in visual world studies, future simulation work should systematically examine how bin size and aggregation affect statistical inference under different degrees of item variance and autocorrelation.

Another limitation of the present work is that our empirical applications and simulation studies relied on a number of simplifications. Across all three studies, we focussed on relatively simple effects, such as departures from baseline and divergences between conditions. More complex designs that cross continuous and factorial predictors remain to be systematically explored and validated (e.g., Galle et al., 2019; McMurray, Aslin, et al., 2008). In addition, the fixation curves assumed in our simulations treated looks as independent samples at each time bin, rather than reflecting the sequential nature of eye movements. Simulations that incorporate such constraints suggest that the observed fixation curves can be biased relative to the underlying generating functions, and noisier than fixation curves obtained with the sampling scheme employed here (McMurray, 2023). Thus, while the present simulations allowed us to compare the GAMM-based and bootstrap-based methods in equivalent, well-controlled conditions, the performance of both methods may differ under more realistic assumptions.

A related, broader limitation of our method (shared with the bootstrap-based method and with many other analytical approaches to the visual world paradigm) is that it relies on fixation curves, that is, proportions of looks over time, rather than on oculomotor events. Because eye movements are discrete, consisting of a sequence of fixations interspersed with shorter saccades, fixation curves are best understood as a statistical abstraction rather than as a direct reflection of the physical events within a trial. Moreover, there is no transparent, one-to-one mapping between cognitive processes (e.g., changes in activation for different lexical candidates) and the timecourse revealed by fixation curves (McMurray, 2023; Teruya & Kapatsinski, 2019). Thus, onset estimates obtained by the GAMM-based method should be interpreted at the level of the fixation curve: they indicate when a manipulation begins to produce a reliable change in the continuous looking probability, without implying a specific account of how (or even when) that influence first appears in the sequence of fixations and saccades.

Nevertheless, we opted to base our method on fixation curves for several reasons. Fixation curve analyses are widely used in the visual world literature, both for timecourse characterisation (McMurray et al., 2010; Mirman, 2014; Porretta et al., 2018; Rigler et al., 2015; Seedorff et al., 2018) and for onset detection (McMurray, Aslin, et al., 2008; Reinisch & Sjerps, 2013). The bootstrap-based method is likewise formulated in terms of fixation curves (Stone, Lago, & Schad, 2021), which makes the comparison between methods more interpretable. In addition, despite the lack of a transparent mapping, both simulation studies (McMurray, 2023) and computational models of spoken-word recognition (Allopenna et al., 1998; Dahan et al., 2001; Hannagan et al., 2013) suggest systematic relations between activation dynamics and fixation curves, supporting their continued use. Finally, fixation curve analyses are more standardised than event-based approaches, for which different metrics are available and may lead to different answers (McMurray, 2023). At the same time, this greater standardisation reflects the current state of methodological development rather than an inherent advantage over approaches based on oculomotor events. Further methodological research on event-based approaches may indeed lead to the development and refinement of analytical workflows, including onset detection measures. More broadly, a long-term goal is to develop generative accounts that link cognitive processes to eye movements in the visual world paradigm, but until these are further specified, we believe fixation curves remain an informative bridge (Magnuson, 2019; McMurray, 2023).

Future extensions of the GAMM-based method

We envision four possible extensions of the GAMM-based method. The first concerns the definition of onsets. Our method defines an onset as the earliest time point at which a predicted fixation curve, or a difference between curves, reliably exceeds its baseline value (i.e., its value at the first time point in the analysis window). This definition accounts for baseline differences while identifying when the effect of interest first becomes reliably detectable. However, other research questions or experimental designs may require different definitions. By way of illustration, suppose that a researcher wants to determine when looks to English phonological competitors begin to decrease in Ito et al.'s (2018) study (see Fig. 3), for example, as a temporal index of cohort inhibition effects (e.g., Allopenna et al., 1998; Huettig & McQueen, 2007). In Study 1, we showed how our method could be adapted to detect the onset of decreases and not only increases in the proportion of target looks. However, the GAMM-based method detects the first increase or decrease (i.e., the earliest onset), but ignores later ones. Thus, in order to estimate when looks to English competitors begin to decrease, the criterion would have to be modified-for example, to detect the time point at which there is a significant reduction relative to the preceding peak. More generally, future versions of the GAMM-based method should allow users to provide custom criteria that best suit their specific research questions.

A second possible extension of the GAMM-based method is the estimation of participantlevel onsets. Such estimates would allow researchers to test whether individuals exhibit earlier or later onsets and to quantify inter-individual variability in effect timing. Our previous (unpublished) attempts to apply the bootstrap-based method of Stone, Lago, and Schad (2021) at the participant level have generally failed, due to large uncertainty in the resulting onset estimates. We expect the GAMM-based method to be easier to extend in this direction, because GAMMs can predict participant-specific fixation curves from the random-effects parameters. The same posterior simulation procedure that we currently apply to the grouplevel fixation curves could also be applied to these participant-specific curves to obtain an onset distribution for each participant. An advantage of using random-effects estimates is that they are less prone to overfitting, because they reflect a compromise between each participant's empirical data and the population-level curve (in the mixed-effects modelling literature, random effects are said to "borrow strength" from the population, Baayen et al., 2008; Kliegl, 2011; Kliegl et al., 2010). Given that participant-level visual world data are typically much noisier and sparser than aggregated data, this approach is a promising avenue for obtaining participant-level onsets. These onset estimates could then be used as participant-level indices in downstream individual differences analyses (e.g., hierarchical regression or mediation), following recent proposals (McMurray et al., 2025).

A third possible extension would be to apply the GAMM-based onset detection procedure directly to oculomotor events rather than fixation curves. For example, eye movement data could be coded in terms of whether a saccade was launched towards a target object, allowing a binomial GAMM to estimate the probability of a target-directed saccade and how it varies over time. The posterior simulation and onset detection procedure developed here could then, in principle, be applied to this saccade-based timecourse to estimate when an experimental manipulation first influences the probability of launching a saccade towards a target image. Such an extension would provide an onset measure more directly tied to an oculomotor event and would be conceptually related to existing onset detection methods based on saccadic latencies (Altmann, 2011; Salverda et al., 2014). However, the implementation and validation of this extension would require a separate investigation.

Finally, we believe that the GAMM-based method is not limited to visual world data, but can be adapted to experimental techniques such as pupillometry and event-related potentials. GAMMs are already used in analyses of data from those techniques (Meulman et al., 2023; Van Rij et al., 2019), partly due to their ability to capture non-linear effects and account for autocorrelation. In principle, the same principles that underlie our method (i.e., posterior simulation from a fitted model and onset detection based on a criterion) can be applied to any technique that generates timeseries data to obtain estimates of temporal onsets and their uncertainty.

Conclusion

We introduced a novel GAMM-based method for detecting the onset of experimental effects in visual world eye-tracking. Through applications to empirical datasets and simulation studies, we demonstrated that our method offers substantial advantages over previous onset detection approaches, particularly the bootstrap-based method proposed by Stone, Lago, and Schad (2021). Our results showed that the GAMM-based method yielded more accurate onset estimates and generally better CI coverage than the bootstrap-based method. Moreover, our method integrates onset detection with modelling fixation curves over time within a single statistical framework. Nevertheless, our simulations showed that both methods can produce systematic delays in onset detection, which can in turn affect comparisons between conditions when their fixation curves differ in steepness. We recommend the adoption of the GAMM-based method in future psycholinguistic research and provide a user-friendly R package to facilitate its use (available at https://gitlab.com/jlverissimo/onsets). By enabling more accurate estimation of effect timing in the visual world paradigm, our method can contribute to advancing theories of prediction and language comprehension.

Study 2: Reanalysis of Ito et al. (2018)

Table S3 shows the difference curve onset estimates and their comparison, as reported in Study 2 in the main manuscript using the default evidence-based criterion. Table S4 reports the corresponding estimates obtained with the four magnitude thresholds. In both tables, onset distributions are summarised by their medians and 95% HDIs. Onsets were detected earlier with the magnitude threshold criterion, both for the target versus unrelated and the English versus unrelated divergences. This likely reflects the relatively high uncertainty of the model-predicted fixation curves in this dataset, given its modest sample size (24 participants and 4 sentences per participant per condition). Thus, the evidence-based criterion, which is based on a one-sided confidence interval, is more stringent than the magnitude thresholds examined here. As in Study 1, a magnitude threshold of zero resulted in onset distributions concentrated at the very beginning of the critical window (here, 200-1000 ms), and consequently extremely narrow intervals at that boundary. Nevertheless, the qualitative conclusions about the comparison of onsets with the magnitude-based criteria were similar to those obtained with the evidence-based criterion: across the positive magnitude thresholds, there was a small tendency for an earlier onset of predictive looks to the target object than to the English competitor, but there was not enough statistical evidence for a difference between the two difference curve onsets.

The bootstrap-based method showed substantially more bias than the GAMM-based method for every effect and in every scenario. Estimates of onset 1 (shallower) were delayed by 62-232 ms, whereas estimates of onset 2 (steeper) showed smaller delays, with bias of 35-127 ms. Estimates of the comparison between onsets undershot the underlying difference (i.e., zero) by 26-105 ms. Bias was largest for the divergence between conditions (81-330 ms later than its underlying value). As in Simulation 1, bootstrap-based estimates became more accurate for larger sample sizes.

Variance. As in Simulation 1, we calculated the SDs of estimates across simulations as a measure of each method's variability (Fig. 9). Across all effects and scenarios, SDs ranged from 7 to 82 ms for the GAMM-based method and 7-48 ms for the bootstrap-based method. The GAMM-based estimates were more variable at the smallest sample size, particularly for the divergence between conditions, but differences between the two methods became much smaller at the medium and large sample sizes.

The average widths of the 95% CIs showed a similar pattern (Appendix S4 in the Supplementary Materials). Across scenarios, average CI widths ranged from 29 to 361 ms for the GAMM-based method and from 30 to 247 ms for the bootstrap-based method. GAMM-based intervals were somewhat wider, with the largest differences between methods at the smallest sample size.

Root mean squared error. The GAMM-based method showed consistently lower RMSE than the bootstrap-based method across all effects, sample sizes, and noise levels (simple onsets: 9-102 ms vs. 36-237 ms; onset comparison: 15-64 ms vs. 29-109 ms; see Appendix S5 in the Supplementary Materials). The largest differences were observed for the divergence between conditions (21-84 ms vs. 82-332 ms). Thus, when considering bias and variability together, the GAMM-based method showed a clear advantage in overall estimation accuracy.

Coverage. Figures 10 and 11 display the empirical coverage of the GAMM-based and bootstrap-based methods. For the GAMM-based method, 95% coverage of the simple onsets ranged from 54% to 92%, with higher coverage under lower noise and at smaller sample sizes. Coverage of the onset comparison ranged from 74% to 95%, whereas coverage of the divergence was more stable, ranging from 90% to 91%. The bootstrap-based method showed very poor coverage of the simple onsets, with only 0%-5% of the 95% CIs containing the underlying value for onset 1 (shallower) and 0%-10% for onset 2 (steeper). Coverage of the onset comparison was higher, but still below nominal levels, ranging from 35% to 90%. Coverage of the divergence was especially poor, at essentially 0% in every scenario. Thus, coverage was below its nominal level for several effects and scenarios for both methods, although it was higher for the GAMM-based method than for the bootstrap-based method in every scenario.

Appendix: Supplementary Materials for "A novel method for detecting the onset of experimental effects in visual world eye-tracking"

João Veríssimo 1 & Sol Lago 2 1 School of Arts and Humanities, University of Lisbon 2 Goethe University Frankfurt Appendix S1. Robustness checks using magnitude threshold criteria

In the main analyses, onsets are defined using the evidence-based criterion described in the "Overview of the novel GAMM-based method" section, which anchors onset detection to evidential strength (via a one-sided confidence interval). As noted in the manuscript, a potential implication of this approach is that onset estimates can depend on the uncertainty around the estimated trajectory. To assess the sensitivity of the empirical conclusions to the choice of onset criterion, we additionally re-estimated onsets using a magnitude threshold variant of the GAMM-based method.

Under the magnitude criterion, an onset is detected when the (simulated) fixation curve exceeds its baseline value by a fixed amount on the modelled log-odds scale. In Studies 1 and 2, we examined four threshold values: 0, 0.05, 0.1, and 0.15 log-odds. For illustration, assuming a baseline probability of 50%, these correspond to increases in probability of approximately 0%, 1.25%, 2.5%, and 3.74%, respectively. Lower thresholds allow detected onsets to remain closer to the point at which the fixation curve first departs from baseline, but are more sensitive to small fluctuations around the baseline. Higher thresholds provide greater protection against such fluctuations, at the cost of yielding later onset estimates (cf. McMurray et al., 2008; Miller et al., 1998; Ulrich & Miller, 2001).

Study 1: Reanalysis of Stone, Veríssimo, et al. (2021)

Table S1 shows the onset estimates and their comparison, as reported in Study 1 in the main manuscript using the default evidence-based criterion. Table S2 reports the corresponding estimates obtained with the four magnitude thresholds. In both tables, onset distributions are summarised by their medians and 95% HDIs. Overall, the results were similar across the positive magnitude thresholds and the default evidence-based criterion, although onset estimates varied with threshold magnitude, being detected later for larger thresholds. As with the default evidence-based criterion, all positive magnitude thresholds yielded significantly earlier onsets in the match than in the mismatch condition. At a threshold of zero, however, the comparison was not significant; this was likely because the simple onset distributions were substantially wider and extended to the very beginning of the critical window.

Figure 1.

Figure 1. Steps of the GAMM-based onset detection method. (1) Predicted proportions of looks based on a fitted GAMM. Shaded areas represent 95% CIs. Crosses represent empirical proportions. (2) Examples of simulated curves from the fitted GAMM. The figure includes only a small number of curves for illustration, but we recommend a minimum of 2,000 simulations for stable results (the analyses in the current paper used 10,000 simulations). Two of the curves are highlighted in black. (3) Dots represent the detected onset for the two highlighted curves. Onset detection takes place in log-odds (the modelled scale in a binomial model), although it is represented in the figure in proportions. (4) Distribution of estimated temporal onsets over all simulations. The dot and error bar represent the median and the 95% HDI.

In the mgcv R package, the response variable is specified as two columns containing counts of target and non-target looks, as such: cbind(target_looks, total_looks -target_looks).

Some parametric non-linear approaches do include an explicit steepness parameter that can be compared across conditions or groups(McMurray et al., 2025). However, obtaining a null result in such a comparison would not establish that steepness is equal, because lack of significance does not license affirming the null hypothesis (e.g.,Altman & Bland, 1995). More importantly, the key issue is what magnitude of steepness difference can be tolerated before Type I error rates become unacceptably inflated, a question that cannot be answered without further simulation work.
